new_statements.translation: p. 246: 'Among the distinguishing features of Chirag, Kajtag and the languages of the southern group one should note the presence of geminate consonants [and] distinctive (meaning-differentiating) stress…'; p. 252 Chirag minimal pairs by stress: gále 'boy' ~ galé 'boys', arčúkːe 'rick' ~ arčukːé 'ricks'; p. 253: 'In ten of the idioms studied, stress moves onto the plural marker' (Chirag among them, p. 254); Table 3 p. 266, Chirag row: fixed stress: no; distinctive stress: yes; stress on the plural marker: yes; the other properties (stress marking the short participle, the masdar, the oblique stem; final closed syllable; second syllable) unknown ('?').

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (nouns: free/mobile stress with minimal pairs; verbs: initial): Moroz confirms distinctive, non-fixed noun stress for Chirag with stress minimal pairs and adds the morphological rule that the plural marker carries the stress (gále/galé, arčúkːe/arčukːé), classing Chirag with Kajtag and South Dargwa against the fixed-stress northern idioms. Silent on verbs. His Chirag evidence is second-hand from Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 (already read held by the project), so it is corroboration by the same primary data, not an independent source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chirag (like Kajtag and the southern Dargwa idioms, unlike the northern/literary group) has non-fixed, distinctive nominal stress; the only regularity Moroz can assert for Chirag is morphological: in the plural the stress falls on the plural marker/final vowel (gále -> galé). His Chirag data are taken from Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990: 281, 335; he has no own Chirag field data, so the syllable-structure generalisations (final closed syllable, second-syllable default) found for Tanti/Qunqi/Ashty are left '?' for Chirag. The chapter treats nouns only; it says nothing about Chirag verb stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None specific to Chirag; the general caveat (p. 254–255) that 'stress moves to the plural marker' is in many examples indistinguishable from 'stress moves to the last syllable', full proof requiring non-absolutive plural forms, which are given only for Qunqi, Xuduc, Ashty and Icari, not for Chirag.
new_statements.identity_note: Chirag = the Dargwa lect of the village Chirag (Agul district, Dagestan), treated by Moroz 2014 as a separate branch of Dargwa ('чирагский язык') following Koryakov 2012, with data from Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 (с. Чираг); Ganenkov & Maisak list 'Chirag' under Dargwa in Fig. 3.1 and (ch. 1 of the same Handbook) call it the most divergent Dargwa variety (~2,000 speakers).

tone_statements.summary: Second-hand report: Chirag was analysed (1978) as having a tonal contrast confined to the stressed syllable (Kodzasov-school 'tone on stressed syllables' type, typically H/L/R/F), never instrumentally verified; the author treats the analysis as uncertain (possibly phonation rather than pitch).

tone.quote: The Dargwa prosodic system is not yet sufficiently described. Judging by the descriptions, most modern Dargwa dialects have a system of morphologically fixed dynamic accent; data collected by the MSU expedition allows us to suggest the presence of other prosodic features (phonations) as well. [p. 90:] We have all reason to think that the PNC word was characterized by tonal accentuation; this is confirmed by the data of the PWC accent system reconstructed by V. A. Dybo (see [Dybo 1977, 1989]), as well as by the discovery of tonal accent systems in modern East Caucasian languages (see [Kibrik-Kodzasov-Starostin 1978]).
tone.locator: p. 121, sec. 1.7.3 'Root structure and prosody' (last paragraph of the Dargwa section 1.7); p. 90, sec. 1.1.3.4 'Prosody'
tone.summary: No tone claimed for Dargwa (incl. Chirag): morphologically governed dynamic stress plus word-level phonation features; tonal systems are attributed to other East Caucasian branches and left undescribed.
